title: NAU-CSC 111/NAU-SEN: Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens and Strategies for Connectives
subject: NAU-CSC111/NAU-SEN 111
description: A practice CBT exam for NAU-CSC 111/NAU-SEN

questions.question: Modus Tollens is valid because it reflects the truth of the:
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens has the form P → Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P. Its validity comes from the equivalence P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P — i.e. the contrapositive of the original implication. Option A (converse, Q → P) is not equivalent. Option B (inverse, ¬P → ¬Q) is also not equivalent. Option D (conjunction) is a connective, not an inference rule. Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original, which is why Modus Tollens is sound.

questions.question: 'If it is a bird, it has wings. It has wings, therefore it is a bird.' This is:
questions.explanation: The form is P → Q (bird → wings), Q (has wings), therefore P (is a bird) — affirming the consequent. This is a fallacy: the premise "has wings" could be satisfied by a bat, an insect, or a plane. Option A (Modus Ponens) would require affirming P ("it is a bird"), not Q. Option C (Modus Tollens) would require denying Q ("it does not have wings"). Option D (denying the antecedent) would require denying P ("it is not a bird").

questions.question: The rule ((P → Q) ∧ (Q → R)) → (P → R) is known as:
questions.explanation: Hypothetical Syllogism — also called "chain argument" or "transitivity of implication" — lets you chain two implications sharing a middle term: from P → Q and Q → R, conclude P → R. Option B (disjunctive syllogism) is from P ∨ Q and ¬P to conclude Q. Option C (conjunction) is from P and Q to conclude P ∧ Q. Option D (exportation) is (P ∧ Q) → R ≡ P → (Q → R).

questions.question: Which rule allows you to infer Q from (P ∨ Q) and ¬P?
questions.explanation: Disjunctive Syllogism: from P ∨ Q and ¬P, conclude Q. Intuition: "one of P or Q is true, and P is false, so Q must be true." Option A (Modus Ponens) needs an implication P → Q, which is not present here. Option C (absorption) is P → Q ≡ P → (P ∧ Q). Option D (addition) is P ⊢ P ∨ Q. Only the disjunctive syllogism fits the P ∨ Q, ¬P premises.

questions.question: If an argument is 'Sound,' it must be valid and its premises must be:
questions.explanation: Soundness = validity (the logical form is correct) plus all premises actually being true. A valid argument with false premises can still be valid — it just isn't sound. Option A (proven) is stronger than needed: premises need only be true, they don't have to have been proved. Option C (consistent) prevents contradiction but does not by itself make premises true. Option D (finite) is irrelevant.

questions.question: Modus Tollens is valid because the implication P → Q is logically equivalent to its:
questions.explanation: The equivalence P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P is the logical foundation of Modus Tollens: since ¬Q → ¬P is a valid form of the original, denying Q and deriving ¬P is a legitimate move. Option A (converse Q → P) is not equivalent. Option B (inverse ¬P → ¬Q) is not equivalent. Option D (conjunction) is a separate connective with no bearing on implication.

questions.question: The fallacy of 'Affirming the Consequent' is represented by the argument:
questions.explanation: Affirming the consequent: from P → Q and Q, infer P. This is the fallacy — Q can be true for reasons unrelated to P. Option A is Modus Ponens (valid). Option C is Modus Tollens (valid). Option D is denying the antecedent, another fallacy but not the one asked about. Option B is the correct answer.

questions.question: Which rule allows the transition from P and Q to P ∧ Q?
questions.explanation: Conjunction introduction: from P and Q as separate premises, conclude P ∧ Q. Option A (simplification) goes the other way: P ∧ Q ⊢ P (or Q). Option C (addition) is P ⊢ P ∨ Q. Option D (absorption) is P → Q ≡ P → (P ∧ Q). The direction distinguishes conjunction introduction from simplification.

questions.question: The rule of 'Disjunctive Syllogism' states that from (P ∨ Q) and ¬P, we can infer:
questions.explanation: Disjunctive syllogism: P ∨ Q and ¬P together imply Q. "Either P or Q; not P; therefore Q." Option A (P ∧ Q) would require both P and Q to be true — but we know P is false. Option C (¬Q) contradicts the conclusion. Option D (P → Q) is an implication, not the standard conclusion of disjunctive syllogism.

questions.question: Hypothetical Syllogism is the logical basis for which type of reasoning?
questions.explanation: Hypothetical Syllogism chains implications: P → Q, Q → R, therefore P → R. It is the logical foundation of transitive reasoning — any argument that proceeds in steps, each step feeding into the next, relies on it. Option A (circular reasoning) is a fallacy — assuming what you're trying to prove. Option C (base case) belongs to induction. Option D (indirect contradiction) is proof by contradiction, unrelated.

questions.question: Modus Ponens is a valid inference rule that can be summarized as:
questions.explanation: Modus Ponens (from P → Q and P, infer Q) works by affirming the antecedent — the "if" part of the implication is confirmed true, so the "then" part follows. Option A (affirming the consequent) is the related fallacy (from Q and P → Q, infer P). Option C (denying the antecedent) is another fallacy (from ¬P and P → Q, infer ¬Q). Option D (denying the consequent) is the description of Modus Tollens, a different valid rule.

questions.question: Given (P → Q) and ¬Q, we conclude ¬P via:
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens: P → Q, ¬Q, therefore ¬P. The mnemonic: deny the consequent (¬Q), conclude the denial of the antecedent (¬P). Option A (Modus Ponens) would need P instead of ¬Q. Option C (addition) is P ⊢ P ∨ Q. Option D (simplification) is P ∧ Q ⊢ P. Only Modus Tollens matches the given premises.

questions.question: The logical fallacy of 'Denying the Antecedent' occurs in which form?
questions.explanation: Denying the antecedent: P → Q, ¬P, therefore ¬Q. This is a fallacy because ¬P does not force ¬Q — Q could be true for reasons other than P. Example: "If it rains, the grass is wet. It does not rain. Therefore, the grass is not wet." Wrong — the sprinkler could be on. Option A is Modus Ponens (valid). Option B is Modus Tollens (valid). Option D is affirming the consequent (another fallacy). Option C is the correct answer.

questions.question: Which rule of inference is the basis for most 'Direct Proofs'?
questions.explanation: A direct proof of P → Q assumes P (the antecedent) and uses logical steps to derive Q (the consequent). That is precisely Modus Ponens: from P → Q and P, conclude Q. Option A (Modus Tollens) underlies contrapositive proofs. Option C (disjunctive syllogism) is a different inference pattern. Option D (hypothetical syllogism) chains implications, useful but not the standard backbone of a direct proof.

questions.question: Modus Tollens is considered sound because it is the logical equivalent of:
questions.explanation: Same core question as Q1/Q6. Modus Tollens (P → Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P) is grounded in the logical equivalence P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P — the contrapositive. Option A (converse Q → P) is not equivalent. Option B (inverse ¬P → ¬Q) is not equivalent. Option D (conjunction) is a connective. Because the contrapositive is equivalent to the original, deriving ¬P from ¬Q is a valid move.

questions.question: Which rule follows the form: (P → Q) ∧ P ∴ Q?
questions.explanation: Modus Ponens: P → Q and P, therefore Q. Option A (Modus Tollens) would use ¬Q, not P. Option C (hypothetical syllogism) chains two implications: P → Q and Q → R. Option D (disjunctive syllogism) uses a disjunction P ∨ Q and ¬P. Only Modus Ponens matches the shape.

questions.question: Which rule follows the form: (P → Q) ∧ ¬Q ∴ ¬P?
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens: P → Q and ¬Q, therefore ¬P. Option A (Modus Ponens) uses P as the second premise. Option C (De Morgan) is a law about negating conjunctions and disjunctions, not an inference rule of this form. Option D (addition) is P ⊢ P ∨ Q. Only Modus Tollens matches the ¬Q → ¬P pattern.

questions.question: Modus Tollens is logically justified by the:
questions.explanation: Same core question as Q1/Q6/Q15. Modus Tollens (P → Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P) draws its soundness from the logical equivalence P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P — the contrapositive. The other options (converse, inverse, conjunction) are not logically equivalent to the original implication and therefore cannot justify Modus Tollens.

questions.question: 'If it rains, the grass is wet. The grass is NOT wet. Therefore, it did NOT rain.' This uses:
questions.explanation: The form is P → Q (rain → wet), ¬Q (not wet), therefore ¬P (not rain) — Modus Tollens. Because the grass is dry, we can conclude with certainty that it did not rain. Option A (Modus Ponens) would need the grass to be wet and then conclude it rained — but wet grass could be from a sprinkler, so that would be the fallacy of affirming the consequent. Option C is not a standard term. Option D is a different fallacy.

questions.question: Which of the following is a logical fallacy?
questions.explanation: The question asks (awkwardly worded) which option is an invalid form — i.e. a fallacy. Affirming the consequent (P → Q, Q, therefore P) is a fallacy. Options A and B are both valid inference rules. Option D (double negation, ¬¬P ≡ P) is a valid equivalence, not a fallacy. Note: the phrase "invalid logical fallacy" is technically redundant — by definition a fallacy is invalid — but the intended answer is clearly C.

questions.question: Which rule of inference follows the form: If P → Q and P are true, then Q is true?
questions.explanation: This is the verbal statement of Modus Ponens: the implication is true, the antecedent is true, so the consequent is true. Option A (Modus Tollens) would use ¬Q as the second premise. Option C chains implications. Option D uses a disjunction. Only Modus Ponens fits "P → Q and P ⟹ Q."

questions.question: Which rule of inference follows the form: If P → Q and ¬Q are true, then ¬P is true?
questions.explanation: This is Modus Tollens stated in English: implication true, consequent false, so antecedent must be false. Option A (Modus Ponens) requires P true. Option C (affirming the consequent) would use Q true to conclude P — invalid. Option D (denying the antecedent) would use ¬P to conclude ¬Q — invalid. Modus Tollens is the only valid rule matching this form.

questions.question: Modus Ponens is Latin for:
questions.explanation: Modus Ponens literally means "method of affirming" — you affirm the antecedent (P) and thereby affirm the consequent (Q). Option A (method of denying) is the meaning of Modus Tollens — modus tollens = "method of denying." Option C (contradiction) and Option D (induction) are unrelated Latin-derived terms describing different proof techniques.

questions.question: Which of the following is an INVALID argument form?
questions.explanation: Affirming the consequent (P → Q, Q, therefore P) is invalid: Q can be true for reasons unrelated to P. Example: "If it's raining, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. Therefore, it's raining." The ground could be wet from a hose. Options A, B, and D (Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, Disjunctive Syllogism) are all valid inference rules.

questions.question: If the generator is on (P), then there is electricity (Q). There is no electricity (¬Q). Therefore, the generator is not on (¬P). This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Form: P → Q, ¬Q, therefore ¬P — Modus Tollens. Option A (Modus Ponens) would need the generator to be on as a premise. Option B (direct proof) is a proof technique, not an inference rule. Option D (fallacy) is wrong — Modus Tollens is a valid rule. The concrete scenario (generator, electricity) is a classic engineering illustration of Modus Tollens.

questions.question: What are rules of inference?
options: Principles used to derive new statements
questions.explanation: Rules of inference are logical principles that allow you to derive new statements (conclusions) from given statements (premises) in a valid way. Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, Hypothetical Syllogism, Disjunctive Syllogism, Conjunction, Simplification, and Addition are the standard rules. Option B (truth tables) is a tool for checking validity, not a rule of inference. Option C (predicates) belongs to predicate logic. Option D (algebraic simplification) is a related but distinct idea in symbolic manipulation.

questions.question: If the premises are true and the rule of inference is valid, then the conclusion must also be:
questions.explanation: Validity guarantees that whenever the premises are true, the conclusion is true — that is the definition of a valid inference rule. Option A (false) contradicts the definition. Option C (undetermined) would mean the rule is not valid. Option D (tautology) overreaches: the conclusion is true given the premises, but the conclusion itself is not necessarily a tautology (true regardless of premises).

questions.question: Modus Ponens is Latin for:
questions.explanation: Same as Q23. Modus Ponens = "method of affirming" — affirming the antecedent P and inferring Q. Option A is the meaning of Modus Tollens. Options C and D are unrelated. Use this question as a spaced-repetition duplicate of Q23 if both remain in the deck.

questions.question: What is the logical form of Modus Ponens?
options: P → Q, Q → R ∴ P → R
questions.explanation: Modus Ponens = P → Q, P, therefore Q. Option A is Modus Tollens. Option C is Disjunctive Syllogism. Option D is Hypothetical Syllogism. Only Option B matches Modus Ponens: implication + antecedent, infer consequent.

questions.question: If it rains, then the ground will be wet. It is raining. Therefore, the ground is wet. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Form: P → Q (rain → wet), P (it is raining), therefore Q (wet). Modus Ponens. Option A (Modus Tollens) would require the ground to be dry. Option C (hypothetical syllogism) chains two implications, which is not happening here. Option D (disjunctive syllogism) would need a disjunction P ∨ Q. This is the classic everyday Modus Ponens example.

questions.question: If n is even, then n² is even. n is even. Therefore, n² is even. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Form: P → Q, P, therefore Q — Modus Ponens, here applied to a number-theoretic implication. Option A (Modus Tollens) would need "n² is not even" as a premise. Option C (affirming the consequent) would go from "n² is even" to "n is even" (invalid). Option D (denying the antecedent) would go from "n is not even" to "n² is not even" (invalid, and in this specific case actually true but only by a separate theorem — the form itself is invalid).

questions.question: If the user enters the correct password, access is granted. The user entered the correct password. Therefore, access is granted. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Form: P → Q (correct password → access), P (entered correct password), therefore Q (access granted). Modus Ponens, applied to authentication logic — a computer science example. Option A (Modus Tollens) would start from "access is not granted." Option C chains implications. Option D needs a disjunction.

questions.question: Modus Ponens is always valid, regardless of the content of P and Q, as long as:
questions.explanation: Inference rules are valid by form, not by content. Modus Ponens is valid because the pattern (P → Q, P ∴ Q) is truth-preserving — regardless of what P and Q actually mean. Option A (conclusion true) mistakes validity for soundness; you don't check the conclusion, you check the form. Option C (premises false) would make the argument unsound, but it can still be valid (validity ≠ soundness). Option D (simplicity) is irrelevant — complex statements work exactly the same way.

questions.question: Modus Tollens is Latin for:
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens literally means "method of denying" — you deny the consequent (¬Q) and thereby deny the antecedent (¬P). Option B (method of affirming) is Modus Ponens. Options C and D are unrelated Latin-derived terms.

questions.question: What is the logical form of Modus Tollens?
options: P → Q, Q → R ∴ P → R
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens = P → Q, ¬Q, therefore ¬P. Option A is Modus Ponens. Option C is Disjunctive Syllogism. Option D is Hypothetical Syllogism. The mnemonic: deny the consequent, get the denied antecedent.

questions.question: If the generator is on, then there is electricity. There is no electricity. Therefore, the generator is not on. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Form: P → Q, ¬Q, therefore ¬P — Modus Tollens. This is a duplicate of the reasoning in Q25 with slightly different wording. Option A (Modus Ponens) would require the generator to be on. Option C would chain implications. Option D needs a disjunction.

questions.question: If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even. The number is not even. Therefore, the number is not divisible by 4. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Form: P → Q (div by 4 → even), ¬Q (not even), therefore ¬P (not div by 4). Modus Tollens applied to a number-theoretic implication. Option A (Modus Ponens) would need "the number is divisible by 4" as a premise. Option C (affirming the consequent) would go from "even" to "divisible by 4" — invalid, since 6 is even but not divisible by 4. Option D (denying the antecedent) would go from "not divisible by 4" to "not even" — invalid, since 6 is a counterexample.

questions.question: If a program compiles successfully, then there are no syntax errors. There are syntax errors. Therefore, the program did not compile successfully. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Form: P → Q (compiles → no syntax errors), ¬Q (there are syntax errors), therefore ¬P (did not compile). Modus Tollens applied to a computer science scenario. Option A (Modus Ponens) would require successful compilation as a premise. Option C chains implications. Option D needs a disjunction.

questions.question: Modus Tollens is closely related to the contrapositive because:
questions.explanation: P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P is the contrapositive equivalence — the same logical basis that makes Modus Tollens valid. Option A (Q → P) is the converse — not equivalent. Option C (¬P → ¬Q) is the inverse — not equivalent. Option D (P ∧ ¬Q) is the negation of the implication, not equivalent. Only the contrapositive gives us "deny the consequent, deny the antecedent."

questions.question: In the comparison of Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens, which premise is used in Modus Ponens?
questions.explanation: Modus Ponens uses the implication P → Q and the affirmation of its antecedent P, concluding Q. Option A (P → Q and ¬Q) is the premise set for Modus Tollens. Option C (P → Q and Q) would be affirming the consequent, a fallacy. Option D (P → Q and ¬P) would be denying the antecedent, another fallacy.

questions.question: In the comparison of Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens, which premise is used in Modus Tollens?
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens uses the implication P → Q and the negation of its consequent ¬Q, concluding ¬P. Option A is the premise set for Modus Ponens. Option C (P → Q and Q) is affirming the consequent (fallacy). Option D (P → Q and ¬P) is denying the antecedent (fallacy). The paired questions Q40 and Q41 reinforce the distinction.

questions.question: What is the conclusion of Modus Ponens?
questions.explanation: In Modus Ponens (P → Q, P), the conclusion is Q — you affirm the antecedent and thereby derive the consequent. Option A (¬P) is the conclusion of Modus Tollens. Option C (P) is a premise, not the conclusion. Option D (¬Q) would contradict the inference. Knowing which conclusion goes with which rule is a common exam point.

questions.question: What is the conclusion of Modus Tollens?
questions.explanation: In Modus Tollens (P → Q, ¬Q), the conclusion is ¬P — you deny the consequent and thereby deny the antecedent. Option A (Q) is the conclusion of Modus Ponens. Option C (P) is a premise side, not the conclusion. Option D (¬Q) is a premise. Modus Tollens always ends with "not the antecedent."

questions.question: What type of reasoning is Modus Ponens commonly used for?
questions.explanation: Wait — this question is missing options. Formatting note: the source only listed two options (A and B). The parser requires at least 2 options, so it will import, but a 2-option question is unusual. Add options C and D if you want consistency — e.g. "Circular reasoning" and "Inductive reasoning." As originally presented, the correct answer is B (forward reasoning): Modus Ponens starts from a known antecedent and derives a new consequent, moving forward from premise to conclusion. Option A (backward reasoning) is the characteristic of Modus Tollens, which starts from the conclusion (¬Q) and works backward to the antecedent (¬P).

questions.question: What type of reasoning is Modus Tollens commonly used for?
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens starts from the negation of the consequent (¬Q) and works back to the negation of the antecedent (¬P) — backward reasoning. This makes it especially useful when Q is easier to test than P. Example: to show "the generator is not on," it is easier to first observe "there is no electricity." Option A (forward reasoning) characterizes Modus Ponens. Options C and D are unrelated (circular reasoning is a fallacy; inductive reasoning generalizes from observations).

questions.question: The fallacy of Affirming the Consequent has the form:
questions.explanation: Affirming the consequent: P → Q, Q, therefore P. Invalid because Q can be true for reasons other than P — the "if" was only one-way. Option A is Modus Ponens (valid). Option C is Modus Tollens (valid). Option D is denying the antecedent (a different fallacy). Only Option B matches the affirming-the-consequent pattern.

questions.question: The fallacy of Denying the Antecedent has the form:
questions.explanation: Denying the antecedent: P → Q, ¬P, therefore ¬Q. Invalid because ¬P does not force ¬Q — Q could be true from another source. Option A is Modus Ponens (valid). Option B is affirming the consequent (another fallacy). Option C is Modus Tollens (valid). Only Option D matches the pattern. Together with Q46, this covers the two classic conditional fallacies.

questions.question: Understanding incorrect reasoning like Affirming the Consequent and Denying the Antecedent helps:
questions.explanation: Knowing the common fallacies helps you avoid making them in your own arguments and spot them in others'. Option A (prove more theorems) is not the primary purpose — knowing fallacies doesn't give you new proof techniques, it just prevents errors. Option C (truth tables) is a separate tool. Option D (predicates) belongs to predicate logic. The practical value is logical hygiene.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid argument form?
questions.explanation: Modus Ponens is a valid inference rule: from P → Q and P, conclude Q. Options A and B (Affirming the Consequent, Denying the Antecedent) are the two classic conditional fallacies. Option D (circular reasoning) is a fallacy in which the conclusion is assumed among the premises. Only Modus Ponens is valid.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid argument form?
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens is a valid inference rule: from P → Q and ¬Q, conclude ¬P. Options A and B are the two conditional fallacies (affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent). Option D (circular reasoning) is a fallacy where the conclusion is smuggled into the premises. Only Modus Tollens is valid.
